config.editorData:
vSAN network — where is the loss?

Four layers carry vSAN traffic and each can fail independently: RDT, vSAN's own transport; TCP beneath it; the vmknic, which is the kernel port; and the physical NIC. A clean NIC proves nothing about RDT, and a clean RDT proves nothing about the NIC.

Read the layers from the top down and stop at the first one that is unhappy. Latency that appears at RDT but not at TCP is vSAN's own queueing. Loss that appears at the vmknic but not at the NIC is the host, not the fabric.

The last two tables are not from this pack. This pack only measures uplinks that carry vSAN traffic, which on a typical host is two of four, so a standby uplink going bad is invisible to it. vCenter counts every uplink, so those columns close a gap rather than repeat one.

RDT latencies - per host

Renders the vSAN RDT Transport Per Host view.

RDT Network Host Average Latency — Average round-trip latency of vSAN's own transport between hosts. This sits above TCP, so it can be slow while every NIC counter is clean.

RDT Network Host Max Latency — Worst round-trip latency observed. Spikes here matter more than the average -- one stalled transfer blocks whatever was waiting on it.

RDT Network Host Min Latency — Best round-trip latency observed. Useful only as a floor to compare the average against.

RDT Network Average Outbound Queueing Latency — Average time a message waited in the outbound queue before being sent. Queueing, as opposed to time on the wire.

RDT Network Max Outbound Queueing Latency — Worst outbound queueing delay observed.

RDT Network Socket Min Outbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the outbound socket buffer. Low is bad -- this measures headroom remaining, so it reads backwards from every other column. Zero means exhaustion and a stalled transport.

RDT Network Socket Min Inbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the inbound socket buffer. Low is bad, for the same reason.

RDT Network Socket Max Inbound Bytes — Highest free space seen inbound. Context for the minimum beside it.

Keepalive reset (Total) — Lifetime count of keepalive resets: RDT gave up on a peer connection and re-established it. Cumulative since boot, so the number itself means little -- watch whether it is increasing.

Num ready delay (Total) — Lifetime count of delays waiting for a connection to become ready. Cumulative since boot; the trend is the signal.

RDT latencies - per vmknic

Renders the vSAN vmknic RDT Latency view.

RDT Network VNIC Average Latency — Average round-trip latency of vSAN's own transport between hosts. This sits above TCP, so it can be slow while every NIC counter is clean.

RDT Network Cluster Max Latency — Worst round-trip latency observed. Spikes here matter more than the average -- one stalled transfer blocks whatever was waiting on it.

RDT Network Cluster Min Latency — Best round-trip latency observed. Useful only as a floor to compare the average against.

RDT Network Average Outbound Queueing Latency — Average time a message waited in the outbound queue before being sent. Queueing, as opposed to time on the wire.

RDT Network Max Outbound Queueing Latency — Worst outbound queueing delay observed.

RDT Network Socket Min Outbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the outbound socket buffer. Low is bad -- this measures headroom remaining, so it reads backwards from every other column. Zero means exhaustion and a stalled transport.

RDT Network Socket Min Inbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the inbound socket buffer. Low is bad, for the same reason.

Keepalive reset (Total) — Lifetime count of keepalive resets: RDT gave up on a peer connection and re-established it. Cumulative since boot, so the number itself means little -- watch whether it is increasing.

Num ready delay (Total) — Lifetime count of delays waiting for a connection to become ready. Cumulative since boot; the trend is the signal.

TCP error types

Renders the vSAN Host TCP Health view.

TCP TX retransmit (rate) — Segments this host had to send again because they were not acknowledged. The cost of loss somewhere on the path, paid in latency.

TCP RX errors (rate) — Inbound TCP segments rejected as erroneous.

Received Duplicate Acknowledge Rate — Duplicate acknowledgements received. The peer is telling us, repeatedly, that it is still missing something -- an early sign of loss on our outbound path, visible before a retransmit timer fires.

Received Duplicate Packets Rate — Duplicate packets received: the same data arrived twice, usually because a peer retransmitted something that was not actually lost.

Received Out-of-order Packets Rate — Packets arriving out of order. Broadcom treat 0.1% as a warning and 1% as critical. Reordering alone is not loss, but TCP responds to it as though it were.

Sack Received Blocks Rate — SACK blocks received. The peer is reporting holes in what we sent it, so this points at loss on our outbound path. Appears before retransmit timeouts do.

Sack Send Blocks Rate — SACK blocks sent. We are reporting holes in what the peer sent us -- loss on our inbound path. The mirror image of the column above, and reading the pair tells you which direction is losing.

Sack Rexmits Rate — Retransmissions we performed because SACK information told us precisely which segments were missing.

Timeout Drop Rate — Established connections torn down because the retransmission timer expired. The end state of sustained loss: the stack gave up rather than kept trying.

Half Open Drop Rate — Connections dropped mid-handshake, in SYN_RCVD -- a SYN arrived, the reply went out, the confirmation never came. Reads 7-9% on a healthy cluster here and the denominator is undocumented, so do not treat a non-zero value as a fault until that is understood.

TCP Send Zero Window (Total) — Times this host told a peer to stop sending because its receive buffer was full. Not a network fault -- the network delivered and the host could not consume. Look up the stack at CPU and at the vSAN layers, not at the wire.

TCP Errors (Total) — Total TCP errors recorded by this host's stack since boot.

pNIC stats - vSAN uplinks

Renders the vSAN pNIC Errors view.

pNIC RX Missed Error — The NIC's receive ring had no free descriptor, so the packet was dropped before the driver ever saw it. The clearest single sign that a NIC is being overrun. Distinct from a drop (discarded higher up) and an error (arrived damaged).

pNIC RX CRC Error — The frame arrived damaged and failed its checksum. Almost always physical: cable, connector, optic or port. Not a capacity problem.

pNIC RX Generic Error — Receive errors not attributed to a more specific counter. Useful as a catch-all; look to the specific counters first.

pNIC RX FIFO Error — The NIC's own on-chip buffer overflowed before it could move packets across PCIe into host memory. The NIC could not hand data over fast enough.

pNIC RX Buffer Overflow Error — Receive buffer overrun. Driver-dependent and often moves with FIFO errors; both mean the receive path could not keep up.

pNIC TX Carrier Error — Carrier lost while transmitting -- a physical link problem. Check the port, cable and link negotiation.

pNIC TX Generic Error — Transmit errors not attributed to a more specific counter.

Inbound Packet Drop Rate of pNic vSwitch Port — The vSwitch discarded inbound packets for this port. A small, constant rate is usually normal: broadcast and multicast traffic the switch has nowhere to deliver. A rate that changes is the signal, not its presence.

Outbound Packet Drop Rate of pNic vSwitch Port — The vSwitch discarded outbound packets for this port.

pNic 802.3x Pause Rate — 802.3x pause frames. These are flow control -- the host and the switch asking each other to slow down. No direction is available, so a non-zero value cannot distinguish 'this host is drowning' from 'the fabric is congested'. Check flow control is even enabled on the uplink before reading a zero as healthy.

IO chain drops — Packets dropped inside the ESXi IO chain, above the NIC and below the vSwitch port.

IO chain RX drops — Inbound packets dropped inside the ESXi IO chain.

IO chain TX drops — Outbound packets dropped inside the ESXi IO chain.

pNIC RX Missed Error (Total) — Lifetime count of missed receive errors since the host booted. The rate columns answer is it happening now; this answers has this NIC ever been bad. A NIC reading 0% now with thousands here has a history worth knowing.

pNIC RX CRC Error (Total) — Lifetime count of CRC errors since boot.

pNIC PFC Count (Total) — Lifetime count of priority flow control frames since boot.

Port TX packets (Total) — Packets transmitted on this vSwitch port. Context, not a fault -- an error count means nothing without knowing the traffic it happened against.

vmknic - the kernel port

Renders the vSAN vmknic view.

Outbound Packet Discard Rate — Proportion of outbound packets discarded at the host network layer.

Inbound Packet Discard Rate — Proportion of inbound packets discarded at the host network layer, across all of this host's vSAN traffic rather than one uplink.

Throughput Inbound — Inbound throughput for this host's vSAN traffic. Context for the error columns.

Throughput Outbound — Outbound throughput for this host's vSAN traffic.

Inbound Packets Per Second — Inbound packets per second.

Outbound Packets Per Second — Outbound packets per second.

Port RX packets — Packets received on this kernel port. Cumulative since boot, and context for the loss rates rather than a fault in itself.

Port TX packets (Total) — Packets transmitted on this vSwitch port. Context, not a fault -- an error count means nothing without knowing the traffic it happened against.

Inbound Packet Drop Rate of vSwitch Port — The vSwitch discarded inbound packets for this port. A small, constant rate is usually normal: broadcast and multicast traffic the switch has nowhere to deliver. A rate that changes is the signal, not its presence.

Outbound Packet Drop Rate of vSwitch Port — The vSwitch discarded outbound packets for this port.

Host network - all vSAN

Renders the vSAN Host Network view.

Network Inbound Packet Discard Rate — Proportion of inbound packets discarded at the host network layer, across all of this host's vSAN traffic rather than one uplink.

Network Outbound Packet Discard Rate — Proportion of outbound packets discarded at the host network layer.

Inbound Packet Drop Rate of vSAN Host Port — The vSwitch discarded inbound packets for this port. A small, constant rate is usually normal: broadcast and multicast traffic the switch has nowhere to deliver. A rate that changes is the signal, not its presence.

Outbound Packet Drop Rate of vSAN Host Port — The vSwitch discarded outbound packets for this port.

Network Inbound Throughput — Inbound throughput for this host's vSAN traffic. Context for the error columns.

Network Outbound Throughput — Outbound throughput for this host's vSAN traffic.

Network Inbound Packets Per Second — Inbound packets per second.

Network Outbound Packets Per Second — Outbound packets per second.

Every uplink - from vCenter

Renders the vSphere Host Uplinks and Load view.

Uplink RX Errors, All NICs — Inbound errors summed across every uplink on the host, counted by vCenter rather than by this pack. This pack only measures uplinks that carry vSAN traffic, which on this cluster is two of four per host, so a standby uplink going bad is invisible to it. This column is here to close that gap.

Uplink RX Dropped, All NICs — Inbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Errors, All NICs — Outbound errors across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Dropped, All NICs — Outbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Host Network Throughput — Total host network throughput, all uplinks and all traffic types. Context for the error columns and a check on whether vSAN is a large or a small share of what this host is doing.

Host CPU Usage — Host CPU usage from vCenter. On the screen so that vSAN latency can be read against host load: a saturated host produces vSAN latency that is not a vSAN problem.

Host CPU Contention — Proportion of time virtual machines waited for CPU. This, not usage, is the contention signal -- a host can be busy without anything waiting, and can make things wait while looking only moderately busy.

Host Memory Consumed — Proportion of host memory consumed.

Host Memory Swap-In Rate — Rate at which the host is reading memory back from disk. Any sustained non-zero value is serious: it means memory was overcommitted far enough to page, and every latency figure on every other panel becomes unreliable while it continues.

Host Uptime — Host uptime. Relevant here because many counters in this pack are cumulative since boot, so a recently rebooted host has small totals for reasons that have nothing to do with health.

CMMDS - cluster membership

Renders the vSAN CMMDS Network view.

Read Outbound — Cluster directory messages sent by this host. CMMDS is how hosts agree on cluster membership and object placement; if it cannot talk, the cluster partitions, and that happens before any IO metric moves.

Read Inbound — Cluster directory messages received.

Read Outbound Throughput — Bytes per second of outbound cluster directory traffic. Small and steady by nature -- a sudden rise usually means membership churn.

Read Inbound Throughput — Bytes per second of inbound cluster directory traffic.

Group Outbound Unicast — Unicast membership messages sent. Modern vSAN uses unicast for membership, so this is the column that should be moving.

Group Inbound — Membership messages received.

Group Outbound Unicast Throughput — Bytes per second of outbound unicast membership traffic.

Group Inbound Throughput — Bytes per second of inbound membership traffic.

Group Outbound Multicast — Multicast membership messages sent. Zero is expected on any cluster since vSAN 6.6, which moved membership to unicast. Non-zero means a legacy configuration.

Group Outbound Multicast Throughput — Bytes per second of outbound multicast membership traffic. Expected to be zero.
